claim: Information order should follow the reader's open question rather than a fixed beat list.
counterexamples: Scientias states the finding first and answers questions the reader has not yet formed (14/25); it works at 650 words
owner_alignment: aligned (leave intellectual work to the reader)
engine_relevance: Story Architect: reader_now_wonders per beat

claim: Explanation is placed after the reader has a reason to need it; the term may be labelled after the ramp.
sources: CT-24 Carl Zimmer, 'Explaining Complexity': find 'the minimum amount of explanation required'
counterexamples: CX-12 glosses every term at first mention in sentence one; contested-subject teaching (CT-07, Zimmer) wants the debate stated upfront

CT-29: Sebastian Junger 'includes technical fishing and boat terms with no definitions, because he believes it makes the piece flow but doesn't feel it integral to explain' - deliberate non-glossing for texture
engine_relevance: Story Architect: concept_introduced ordering; definitions timing

claim: Concrete<->abstract movement is a pacing instrument: a stalled passage is a signal to change abstraction level.
counterexamples: CX-09 stays LOW for most of its length and does not stall
engine_relevance: Story Architect: abstraction level per beat

claim: Narrative material is acquired by reporting before writing, not composed at writing time.
engine_relevance: Research Pack: explicit narrative-material need; Worth Gate: form choice as the accommodation when material is thin

claim: Strong texts vary article form; structural craft is form-dependent.
engine_relevance: ARTICLE_TYPES is a length scale, not a form taxonomy

claim: Concrete facts are allowed to stand before interpretation.
counterexamples: BR-02 interprets inside the same paragraph in the prescription sections
owner_alignment: aligned (do not compress the reader into the insight)
engine_relevance: Continuity: do not attach a verdict to every evidence sentence

claim: Excessive semantic compression is measurable and strong accessible prose largely avoids it.
counterexamples: SC-02 opening sentence carries five kinds of information at once, and works, because none of them is an interpretation
owner_alignment: the owner's own diagnosis, now with numbers
engine_relevance: reportable diagnostic on the draft: single-clause share, commas/sentence, >=4-clause share

claim: Numbers are converted to a person, a familiar unit, a time series or a scale.

counterexamples: BR-13 leaves 188.8% unexplained
engine_relevance: Story Architect: number handling declared per fact

claim: Endings are often improved by stopping earlier rather than writing a stronger final move.
counterexamples: BR-14 cannot end earlier; CX-02, CX-08, CX-09 endings are load-bearing
engine_relevance: an upstream-truncation check on the finished draft

claim: The idea may be implicit or explicit; the deciding variable is reader need, not house style.

owner_alignment: aligned (lens should emerge naturally where possible)
engine_relevance: PR62 lens_realization IMPLICIT/EXPLICIT/EITHER is correct as designed

counterexamples: the entire control group's dominant practice supports the default
owner_alignment: partially conflicts: owner wants concrete reality before interpretation, which is a different claim from concrete-first

claim: Announcing the thesis is not a defect; placement is the decision.
counterexamples: CX-09 and CX-02 have no explicit thesis and are excellent
owner_alignment: conflicts with owner's Bregman-style 'no thesis announcement' preference; note that Bregman himself announces

claim: Visible CONTENT transitions (head-to-tail echo, contrast turn, 'But wait', dated launch-pad after a section break) are taught craft used in narrative features. Visible OUTLINE transitions (announcing the structure) are a genre marker of the argumentative essay. The distinction is not visible vs invisible.
sources: control exemplars near-zero; annotators praise head-to-tail and invisible braiding (CX-08 annotations 7,16; CX-09 annotation 21)
CT-25 The Open Notebook 'Good Transitions' (Draxler, Lloyd, Yam, Khamsi, Fox, Ananthaswamy)
CT-21 Berkeley syllabus lists 'signposts' as an element to master
counterexamples: CT-25 uses the word 'signpost' approvingly of a short declarative paragraph opener; Lloyd calls head-to-tail transitions a deliberate 'control mechanism ... more intentionally, more aggressively'; her caution is USE SPARINGLY, not delete-first
owner_alignment: conflicts with owner's 'avoid visible machine/story scaffolding' if applied to argument forms
engine_relevance: PR62 SIGNPOST_SHAPES flags read/look at/notice/consider/remember/go back/return - the exact class CT-25 teaches as good craft. Keep the detector, give it a published baseline, and separate content transitions from outline transitions.
revision_note: First V2 pass concluded signposting was near-absent from narrative features (0.005/paragraph measured). CT-25, supplied via the V1 seed as C08, shows narrative features use visible transition devices constantly - just not outline-announcing ones. The signpost DETECTOR still discriminates (Jia 0.333/paragraph); it needs a baseline, not a zero threshold. FURTHER CORRECTED on implementation: SIGNPOST_SHAPES flags 0 of 6 devices the source praises and 4 of 4 Jia defects, so no content/outline split in the patterns was needed - the fix was a baseline, not a taxonomy.
acted_on: 2026-09-04 calibration pass 1: signpost rate banded against the published corpus (narrative max 0.025, argument max 0.125) with an optional form parameter, a <10-paragraph abstention and a corpus-derived absolute-count floor of 3

counterexamples: Scientias has zero and is accessible; continuity.py measured 33% in Jia as a defect

acted_on: 2026-09-04 calibration pass 1: solo_ratio demoted to declared telemetry in continuity.writtenness(); docstrings corrected; regression test asserts solo-heavy published-shaped prose is not condemned

claim: A protagonist need not be a person: an animal, an object, a body part, a chart or a concept can carry a piece.
sources: CX-01 (the wave 'almost acts as a character')
counterexamples: CX-07 annotation 12: statistics without a person loses readers
engine_relevance: CARRIERS already permits object/event/place/process - well supported

claim: Provenance about what evidence SHOWS can be reader-facing and useful; provenance about what evidence LACKS is the machine describing itself.
owner_alignment: aligned (avoid source/account language in reader prose)
engine_relevance: the ban on 'does not (establish|say|...)' is exactly right; the ban on the bare phrase 'the evidence' is broader than the craft evidence

claim: Telling the reader what a number does NOT mean is a reader-serving negative statement, distinct from evidence-state commentary.
sources: SC-14 (1.5 degrees is not a tipping point)
scope: Scientias; not observed in the Bregman or control samples
engine_relevance: negative_claim_scan cannot currently distinguish these two shapes

claim: Uncertainty is best carried structurally (a limitations passage) rather than lexically (hedging adverbs).
sources: SC-09 five consecutive limitation paragraphs = ~30% of the article
SC-05 sigma accounting plus no-peer-review note
scope: Scientias science news; untested at Crip Minds length
counterexamples: control exemplars distribute uncertainty through the prose instead and are not criticised for it
engine_relevance: a candidate beat role; no current equivalent

claim: Reconstructed scene is licensed craft, bounded by evidence density and by not implying presence the writer did not have. Superseded in operational detail by F-27.
sources: see F-27 for the three-tier provenance taxonomy
engine_relevance: confirms the safety rule from inside the craft literature; the remedy for thin evidence is form choice or more research, never vividness

claim: Bregman's question density (5.06/1k) and direct address (20.9/1k) are personal signature, not general accessibility traits.
sources: metrics section 5; control 0.87 and 8.02; Scientias 0.91 and 9.89 after boilerplate removal
owner_alignment: the owner names Bregman as primary craft model; this finding says which parts are borrowable
engine_relevance: do not target Bregman's question rate; target his clause load

claim: Accessibility is a low clause load with a wide sentence-length range, not short sentences.
sources: CT-05 (Mullin on long sentences inviting the reader to wander)
engine_relevance: the measurable target in metrics section 3

claim: Research can be fully present in authority and fully absent from the sentence.
sources: BR-01: 38 footnotes for 5,072 words of prose with almost no in-line source machinery
counterexamples: CX-10's transparent methodology block does the opposite and is praised

claim: Two named, incompatible background architectures exist and the choice depends partly on the material reporting yielded.
engine_relevance: the ledger already measures evidence density, which is the deciding input

claim: The reader's objection, written as its own paragraph and answered where it arises, is distinct from the reader's question.
counterexamples: absent from all 12 control exemplars
engine_relevance: a candidate beat role for argumentative forms only

claim: Professional annotators of excellent work spend most of their attention below paragraph level, on verbs and concrete details.
sources: 421 annotations; 45% outside every macro-structural keyword category; CX-05 has six annotations praising individual verbs
scope: indicative only - keyword coding with a 45% residual
engine_relevance: caution about our own priors: we design macro-architecture; the craft literature attends to word choice

claim: A massive explanation can be dispersed through the story, or replaced by narrating how the explanation was discovered.
sources: CT-24 Carl Zimmer: 'it's often a good move to disperse pieces of the explanation throughout your story ... Tell the story of the explanation, rather than giving the explanation itself'
BR-14 (mall experiment -> confound -> India natural experiment)
counterexamples: SC-28 gives a full definitional block at P6 rather than dispersing it - and works, at 650 words
owner_alignment: aligned; a route to difficult ideas without an exposition slab
engine_relevance: a structural option the Story Architect cannot currently express: explanation as a sequence of discovery events rather than an EXPLANATION beat

claim: Scene provenance has three legitimate tiers, and tier 2 - the debriefed observer - is the tier Crip Minds occupies.
sources: CT-27 Lauren Kessler, worked through one published article: (1) direct observation 'I sat quietly in the corner and took notes'; (2) debriefed observer - a scene that 'reads like the product of direct observation, but was not', built from a doctor's second-by-second notes read aloud plus follow-up questions, prior sight of the room, conversations with the daughter; (3) recorded material 'after I watched and rewatched the tape'. Rule: 'A scene can be written only if the journalist has the material, however that material is ever-so-carefully gathered.'
CT-29 Sebastian Junger covered The Perfect Storm 'entirely through second-hand accounts and materials' - 4,765 words, zero direct observation
owner_alignment: aligned; resolves the apparent craft/safety collision from inside the craft literature
engine_relevance: operational form: a scene may be written when a ledger fact is an observer record of that moment, at the granularity being written. This is checkable against the ledger and is stronger than a blanket scene prohibition.

claim: The more intrinsically dramatic the material, the plainer the telling should be.
sources: CT-27 Kessler: 'The narration ... is presented as simply as possible, unadorned by adjectives, adverbs, metaphors, whatever. The moments themselves were dramatic; I did not want to force more drama into the retelling.'
CX-10 annotation 5: 'The more intrinsically dramatic the scene you're describing, the more plainly and simply you're required to tell it.'
counterexamples: CX-01 and CX-09 use lyric description heavily on non-dramatic material, which is consistent: the rule binds where the material is already dramatic
owner_alignment: aligned (plain factual description before interpretive flourish)
engine_relevance: the direct antidote to a 'make every verb evocative' pass; belongs to the Continuity Editor's zero-factual-freedom stage

claim: Structure decisions drive acquisition, not only the reverse: writers decide the story's universe, then work backwards to the material they need.
sources: CT-28 Banaszynski: 'We start with a story vision and purpose in mind. Then we have to back up and think about the pieces-parts we need: X sources, Y observation, Z context. From there, we build forward.'
CT-23 Tom French: 'The moment you decide on the universe of your story, you're making a decision about structure.'
counterexamples: CT-23 Aschwanden: 'The structure falls out of the story itself. I can't outline it in advance' - two accomplished writers with opposite methods in the same source
engine_relevance: PR62 acquires then structures. The teaching says the loop runs both ways, which is what a research-for-story need gate would implement.

claim: The harder the material, the SIMPLER the structure should be.
sources: CT-23 Tom French: 'What you want is for the structure to be as simple as it can be so that the reader has the best chance possible to think about the complexity of what you're trying to get across. The more complex the material, the simpler the structure should be.'
CT-29 Sarah Scoles: 'it's good for the reader, if you're writing about complicated things, to go with a chronological structure'
CT-23: New Yorker writers 'can use any structure they want, but at the end of the day they will change it back to chronological'
counterexamples: CT-07 Rowinska reorganised AWAY from chronology once a debate had more than two camps - so 'simple' does not always mean 'chronological'
engine_relevance: argues against elaborating the Story Architect for difficult material - the direction PR62 has been travelling. The simplest available structure is a design target, not a fallback.

claim: A reader question can be used as a literal section heading, with the explainer block placed after the finding rather than before it.
sources: SC-28: standalone interrogative subheading 'Wat is nitraat en waarom is het zo belangrijk?' at P5, after finding (P0), mechanism (P1) and method (P4); full definition follows at P6-P7, while a light gloss was given in apposition at P0
engine_relevance: two-stage glossing: light gloss at first use, full block when the reader needs depth. Distinct from the single 'EXPLAIN AT FIRST USE' slot in the writer packet.
